title: Hachinohe — 八戸
goal: Understand a coastal shopping scene, count simple items and people, and recognise entrance/exit words.

blocks.text: 八戸
はちのへ — Hachinohe

Hachinohe is on Aomori's Pacific coast and is associated with seafood, coastal scenery, and markets. This is a useful place to connect **海**, which you met on the very first Hokkaido lesson, with **魚**, which we will study today.

**八戸で魚を食べます。**
はちのへで さかなを たべます。
I eat fish in Hachinohe.
Identify the place, the object, and the action. Only the fish word and city name are new. Do not treat the entire sentence as an unrelated string to memorise.

items: **Kanji:** 八 · **Useful meaning/readings:** eight; はち · **Radical/components:** Radical 八, はち. Two spreading strokes · **Learning role:** Review from Hakodate. The character is its own indexing radical; it is not two separate tree branches.

**Kanji:** 戸 · **Useful meaning/readings:** door; と; on コ · **Radical/components:** Radical 戸, と. The modern shape can be recognised as a top horizontal and door-like body · **Learning role:** Encounter. Its historical connection is a single door leaf; the entire shape is the useful clue.

blocks.text: Together: **八戸 / はちのへ**. The の is part of the place name's reading, not the noun-connecting particle written between 八 and 戸. 戸 is read へ in this name; the ordinary door word is 戸 / と.
Do not claim that the city name simply means “eight doors.” We are explaining its characters, not researching the historical naming system in this lesson.

cards.title: 魚: A New Word Connected to 海

blocks.text: **魚** — さかな — fish; common on reading ギョ.

魚 is also its own radical, うお/さかな. The modern character contains a top section, a 田-like body, and four bottom dots **灬**. Its historical shape represents a fish. The bottom dots are not a reason to say every 魚 character is about fire.

**海に魚がいます。**
うみに さかなが います。
There are fish in the sea.
A living fish uses **います**. A prepared fish served as food is the object of **食べます**. The word is the same, but the context and grammar differ.

**魚を買います。**
さかなを かいます。
I buy fish.
The kanji/word connects to nature, shopping, and food. That is the kind of connected knowledge our Journey builds.

cards.title: 口: A Mouth and an Opening

blocks.text: **口** — くち — mouth; on コウ.
口 is its own radical, くち. Its enclosed shape is a useful recognition cue. We do not need to split it into meaningless independent lines.
It also appears in opening/entrance words:

items: **入り口** — いりぐち — entrance.
**出口** — でぐち — exit.

blocks.text: In these words, くち becomes **ぐち**. This is another sound change to learn with the whole word, just as 百 had special forms in Hokkaido.
The word mouth and the idea of an opening are connected, but “exit” cannot be guessed from 口 alone. Look at the other character and learn the compound.

cards.title: 入 and 出: Enter and Leave

items: **Word:** 入る · **Reading:** はいる · **Polite form:** 入ります / はいります · **Meaning:** enter
**Word:** 出る · **Reading:** でる · **Polite form:** 出ます / でます · **Meaning:** leave; go out

blocks.text: **入** is its own radical, いる. Its two strokes are a recognition shape, not the same character as 人 or 八.

**出** is indexed under **凵**, うけばこ, an open-box-shaped radical you encountered with 函. Its modern stacked shape can remind you of movement outward; do not label it “two mountains” as a historical definition.

**店に入ります。**
みせに はいります。
I enter the shop.

**店を出ます。**
みせを でます。
I leave the shop.
Here を marks the place being left, rather than a thing being eaten or bought. This is a small new use in a fixed, useful expression. Do not generalise it to every verb of movement.
You know the written numbers. Now learn the common **〜つ** forms used for many ordinary items:

items: **Count:** 一つ · **Reading:** ひとつ · **Count:** 六つ · **Reading:** むっつ
**Count:** 二つ · **Reading:** ふたつ · **Count:** 七つ · **Reading:** ななつ
**Count:** 三つ · **Reading:** みっつ · **Count:** 八つ · **Reading:** やっつ
**Count:** 四つ · **Reading:** よっつ · **Count:** 九つ · **Reading:** ここのつ
**Count:** 五つ · **Reading:** いつつ · **Count:** 十 · **Reading:** とお

blocks.text: The tenth form is **とお**, without つ. These are different from ordinary いち・に・さん counting.

**りんごを二つ買います。**
りんごを ふたつ かいます。
I buy two apples.

りんごを names the object; 二つ gives the number of items; 買います gives the action. This is a useful general counter, not a promise that Japanese uses 〜つ for everything. Special counters for bottles, books, animals, and other categories will come later.
**いくつ** — how many, for the general item counter.

**りんごをいくつ買いますか。**
りんごを いくつ かいますか。
How many apples will you buy?

**三つ買います。**
みっつ かいます。
I will buy three.
Contrast **いくら** = how much money with **いくつ** = how many items.

A practice note says: **りんご二つ、二百円。**
りんご ふたつ、にひゃくえん。
Two apples, 200 yen.
The count is 二つ; the price is 二百円. They are different kinds of information. The price is a fictional total in our exercise, not a rule about apple pricing.

items: **People:** 一人 · **Reading:** ひとり
**People:** 二人 · **Reading:** ふたり
**People:** 三人 · **Reading:** さんにん
**People:** 何人 · **Reading:** なんにん — how many people?

blocks.text: The first two are special. Do not read 一人 as いちにん or 二人 as ににん in this ordinary counting use.

**店に二人います。**
みせに ふたり います。
There are two people in the shop.

**何人いますか。**
なんにん いますか。
How many people are there?
Hokkaido taught 人 as a person and showed 三人. We are now adding the irregular first two forms. The counting word already refers to people, so the first sentence does not need another 人 noun.

cards.title: どれ and どの Ask “Which?”

blocks.text:
**どれ** stands alone: which one?
**どの + noun** asks which specific noun.

**どれですか。** — どれですか。 — Which one is it?
**どのりんごですか。** — どの りんごですか。 — Which apple is it?

**Learner:** どのりんごですか。
Which apple?
**Guide:** このりんごです。
This apple.
The choice is among visible apples in our practice scene. Both the question and answer use a modifier followed by its noun. Compare **どれですか → これです** when no noun is spoken.
Do not add a noun directly after どれ: “どれりんご” is not the pattern we want.
A shopkeeper may welcome a customer with **いらっしゃいませ**. You can recognise it without being expected to use it as a customer.
Before eating, **いただきます** is a useful customary phrase. After a meal, **ごちそうさまでした** expresses appreciation. They do not translate word-for-word into a single English eating verb.
Our fictional account:

**店に入りました。魚を食べました。店を出ました。**
みせに はいりました。さかなを たべました。みせを でました。
I entered the shop. I ate fish. I left the shop.
The past ending is familiar. Recognise 入・食・出 as the same characters even when their kana endings change.

items: Read 二つ: につ / ふたつ / ふたり.
Read 二人: ににん / ふたつ / ふたり.
Choose “exit”: 入り口 / 出口 / 店.
Complete “Which shop?”: ＿＿店ですか。 どれ / どの / これ.

blocks.text: **Answers:** 1 ふたつ: two items. 2 ふたり: two people. 3 出口. 4 どの: it needs the noun 店.
Build **店に二人います。** Then change the number to 一人. Do you remember the special reading? **店に一人います。** — みせに ひとり います。

items: **Location:** 八戸 — はちのへ. 八 is review; 戸 is an encounter.
**Fish:** 魚 = さかな; living fish use います.
**Signs:** 入り口 = いりぐち; 出口 = でぐち; 口 changes to ぐち.
**Movement:** 店に入ります; 店を出ます.
**Items:** 一つ〜九つ, then 十 / とお. いくつ asks how many items.
**People:** 一人 / ひとり; 二人 / ふたり; 三人 / さんにん.
**Which?:** どれ stands alone; どの needs a noun.
**Courtesy:** いらっしゃいませ is the welcome; いただきます before eating; ごちそうさまでした after eating.
**Review link:** 海 → 魚 → 食; 八 → 八つ; 凵 in 函 and the indexing of 出.

blocks.text: **Aomori's three location lessons are complete. Continue to the Aomori Reading Journey and test before Iwate.**
